2.2.3.j.text: Reference document v1.4.2 has two Z tables. The left-tail table (Z = −4.9 to 0.0) gives P(Z below z); e.g., Z = −1.96 gives 0.02500. A second table titled "Right Tail Area" (Z = 0.00 to 4.9) actually lists the area to the left of Z (0.97500 at 1.96). So P(Z above z) = 1 − (table value for z), or use the left-tail table at −z; P(Z between −z and z) = 2 × (table value) − 1.
2.2.3.j.title: Reading the Z table

2.2.3.k.text: The Z table stops at 4.9, and very small tails print as 0.00000. For 6σ-level questions expect the known 3.4 DPMO rather than a table lookup.

2.3.1.a.text: Accuracy = closeness to the true value. Precision = closeness of repeated measurements to each other.
2.3.1.a.title: Accuracy versus precision

2.3.1.b.text: Resolution (discrimination): measurement increments should be about 1/10 or finer of the tolerance or process spread
2.3.1.b.title: Resolution (discrimination)

2.3.1.d.text: Location errors: bias, linearity, stability. Spread errors: repeatability, reproducibility.
2.3.1.d.title: The five components

2.3.1.f.text: Target analogy: tight cluster far from center = precise but not accurate.
2.3.1.f.title: The target analogy

2.3.2.a.text: Bias = average measured value − reference value
2.3.2.a.title: Bias

2.3.2.b.text: Linearity = how bias changes across the operating range of the gage
2.3.2.b.title: Linearity

2.3.2.c.text: Stability = how bias changes over time (drift); tracked with a control chart on a master part
2.3.2.c.title: Stability

2.3.2.d.text: Corrective action depends on the pattern: calibration or adjustment for bias; a different gage or method for linearity; environment, wear, maintenance, or time effects for stability.
2.3.2.d.title: Corrective action

2.3.2.e.text: "Gage reads higher on larger parts" = linearity. "Gage drifts over weeks" = stability. "Reads consistently high" = bias.
2.3.2.e.title: Name the error

2.3.3.a.text: Repeatability: same operator, same part, same gage (equipment variation)
2.3.3.a.title: Repeatability

2.3.3.b.text: Reproducibility: different operators on the same parts (appraiser variation)
2.3.3.b.title: Reproducibility

2.3.3.f.text: %Tolerance = 6 × GRR / (USL − LSL) × 100. Study spread is 6σ in current guidance; older material used 5.15σ. Check which a question uses.
2.3.3.f.title: % Tolerance

2.3.3.g.text: %Contribution uses variances rather than standard deviations
2.3.3.g.title: % Contribution

2.3.3.h.text: Acceptance (AIAG, as cited by Minitab): under 10% acceptable; 10 to 30% may be acceptable depending on the application, gage cost, and cost of repair; over 30% unacceptable and should be improved.
2.3.3.h.title: Acceptance guidelines

2.3.3.i.text: Number of distinct categories ndc = 1.41 × (part SD / GRR SD). Need ndc ≥ 5. Software truncates ndc to a whole number; do not round up.
2.3.3.i.title: Number of distinct categories (ndc)

2.3.3.j.text: Typical (not mandatory) design: about 10 parts spanning the process range, 3 operators, 2 to 3 repeats, randomized, blinded
2.3.3.j.title: Typical study design

2.3.3.k.text: Crossed vs nested (destructive testing); ANOVA method vs Xbar-R method
2.3.3.k.title: Crossed versus nested; ANOVA versus Xbar-R

2.3.3.l.text: Reading the graphs: R chart by operator (consistency); Xbar chart by operator (should show many out-of-control points, because parts should differ); operator-by-part interaction
2.3.3.l.title: Reading the graphs

2.3.3.m.text: Given the components, compute %GRR and decide if the gage is acceptable.
2.3.3.m.title: Compute %GRR and decide

2.3.3.n.text: %Study Var is on a standard-deviation basis; %Contribution is on a variance basis (about the square). Equivalent cutoffs on contribution are roughly 1% and 9%.
2.3.3.n.title: %Study Var versus %Contribution

2.3.3.o.text: Diagnose the pattern: large repeatability = equipment, fixture, or method; large reproducibility = operator technique, training, or standardization; significant operator × part interaction = inconsistent operator-part behavior
2.3.3.o.title: Diagnose the pattern

2.3.3.p.text: %Study Var marginal but %Tolerance over 30%: for sorting or conformance decisions %Tolerance is more relevant (Minitab); for evaluating process improvements %Study Var is the better precision estimate

2.3.4.a.title: Variable MSA

2.3.4.b.title: Attribute agreement analysis

2.3.4.d.text: AIAG (as cited by Minitab): kappa ≥ 0.75 indicates good agreement. Some software (for example SigmaXL) uses a ≥ 0.9 / 0.7 to 0.9 / < 0.7 rule of thumb, and a '< 0.40 poor' band appears in other texts. Know which source a question implies. Unsure which convention IASSC uses.
2.3.4.d.title: Interpreting kappa

2.3.4.e.title: Typical study design

2.3.4.f.title: Misclassification metrics

2.3.4.g.title: Interpret a kappa table

2.3.4.h.text: Agreement with self and with each other is not accuracy: appraisers can agree and all be wrong. Check agreement against the known standard.
2.3.4.h.title: Agreement is not accuracy

2.3.4.i.text: Fleiss' vs Cohen's kappa; Kendall's coefficient for ordinal data (recognition only)
2.3.4.i.title: Fleiss' versus Cohen's kappa, and Kendall's coefficient

2.4.1.a.text: Spec limits (voice of the customer) vs control limits (voice of the process). They are independent.
2.4.1.a.title: Spec limits versus control limits

2.4.1.d.text: Cpk ≤ Cp always; equal only when the process is centered
2.4.1.d.title: Cpk is never above Cp

2.4.1.e.text: Pp and Ppk use overall (long-term) σ instead of within σ
2.4.1.e.title: Pp and Ppk

2.4.1.f.text: Defining difference: Cp/Cpk use within-subgroup σ; Pp/Ppk use overall σ. 'Short-term' and 'long-term' are shorthand for that.
2.4.1.f.title: The defining difference

2.4.1.g.text: Benchmarks: sigma level (short-term Z) = 3 × Cpk, so Cpk 1.00 ≈ 3σ; 1.33 ≈ 4σ; 1.67 ≈ 5σ; 2.00 ≈ 6σ. With the 1.5σ convention the long-term yield sits 1.5σ lower (Cpk 1.33 ↔ about 6,210 DPMO; Cpk 2.00 ↔ 3.4 DPMO). Cue words matter: 'long-term' or 'with shift' means subtract 1.5; no mention of a shift means read the Z table directly.
2.4.1.g.title: Benchmarks and sigma level

2.4.1.h.text: Z values: Z_USL = (USL − μ)/σ and Z_LSL = (μ − LSL)/σ; convert to PPM out of spec and sum both tails for the total
2.4.1.h.title: Z values and defects

2.4.1.i.text: Stability is a prerequisite for meaningful capability inference. Conventional Cp/Cpk and PPM estimates assume normality; non-normal data need a transformation or a non-normal capability model.
2.4.1.i.title: Assumptions

2.4.1.j.text: Cp ≫ Cpk means centering problem. Low Cp means a variation problem.
2.4.1.j.title: What the gap tells you

2.4.1.k.text: Cpm (Taguchi) penalizes distance from target (glossary only, low exam yield)
2.4.1.k.title: Cpm

2.4.1.l.text: "Cp 1.8, Cpk 0.9": the process is off-center rather than too variable. Center it if the chart is stable. If the chart is unstable, stabilize first.
2.4.1.l.title: "Cp 1.8, Cpk 0.9"

2.4.1.m.text: Compute Cpk from a mean, σ, and two spec limits.
2.4.1.m.title: Compute Cpk from raw numbers

2.4.1.n.text: One-sided specs: Cpu = (USL − μ) / 3σ or Cpl = (μ − LSL) / 3σ; Cpk is the smaller when both exist
2.4.1.n.title: One-sided specs

2.4.1.o.text: Decision matrix: stable and capable = monitor; stable and incapable = reduce variation, recenter, or redesign; unstable and apparently capable = fix special causes first (indices not trustworthy); unstable and incapable = stabilize first
2.4.1.o.title: The decision matrix

2.4.1.p.text: Capability indices computed on an unstable process are not valid; the correct first step is addressing special causes
2.4.1.p.title: Capability on an unstable process

2.4.1.q.text: Reference-sheet formulas: Cp = (USL − LSL) / 6s; Z_upper = (USL − X̄)/s; Z_lower = (X̄ − LSL)/s; Cpk = min(Z_upper/3, Z_lower/3). The sheet uses the sample standard deviation s throughout.
2.4.1.q.title: Reference-sheet formulas

2.4.1.r.text: Cpk from attribute data: Cpk = (1.5 + Z of the proportion good) / 3, with Z read from the Z table
2.4.1.r.title: Cpk from attribute data

2.4.1.s.text: Confidence interval for Cpk: Cpk ± Z(α/2) × √[1/(9n) + Cpk²/(2n − 2)]. The same square root is the standard error of Cpk.
2.4.1.s.title: Confidence interval for Cpk

2.4.2.c.title: Tampering

2.4.2.e.title: Stability comes first

2.4.2.f.title: Stable but incapable versus capable but unstable

2.4.3.e.title: Check stability first

2.4.3.f.text: Defects vs defectives picks the right distribution and chart.
2.4.3.f.title: Defects versus defectives

2.4.3.g.text: Sigma level from DPMO using the Z table: DPMO ÷ 1,000,000 = right-tail area; read Z; add 1.5. Example: 66,807 DPMO gives area 0.06681, Z ≈ 1.5, so 3.0σ.
2.4.3.g.title: Sigma level from DPMO with the Z table

2.4.4.a.text: Ongoing monitoring of capability with control charts (Xbar-R, I-MR, p, u)
2.4.4.a.title: Monitoring with control charts

2.4.4.b.text: Monitor with time-ordered SPC first; re-evaluate capability after a stable period or a process change. Rolling capability indices on an unstable process mislead.

2.4.4.d.title: Run charts

3.1.2.a.text: Continuous: normal, lognormal, Weibull, exponential, uniform
3.1.2.a.title: Continuous distributions

3.1.2.b.text: Discrete: binomial (pass/fail counts), Poisson (defect counts), hypergeometric (sampling without replacement)
3.1.2.b.title: Discrete distributions

3.1.2.c.text: Binomial: P(x) = nCx · p^x · (1−p)^(n−x); mean = np
3.1.2.c.title: Binomial

3.1.2.d.text: Poisson: P(x) = e^(−λ) λ^x / x!; mean = variance = λ
3.1.2.d.title: Poisson

3.1.2.f.text: Sampling distributions: t (heavier tails, df), chi-square (variances), F (ratio of variances)
3.1.2.f.title: Sampling distributions

3.1.2.g.text: Time-to-failure data often follow Weibull or exponential; positively skewed bounded data often lognormal
3.1.2.g.title: Typical uses

3.1.2.h.text: Poisson approximates binomial for small p; normal approximates binomial when both np and n(1−p) are at least 5 (some use 10). Exam rule of thumb.
3.1.2.h.title: Approximations

3.1.2.i.text: Match a scenario to the distribution (defects on a unit = Poisson).
3.1.2.i.title: Match the scenario

3.1.2.j.text: Assumptions: binomial = fixed n, independent trials, constant p; Poisson = counts over a fixed exposure at a constant rate; exponential = time between events; Weibull = flexible failure shape
3.1.2.j.title: Assumptions behind each

3.1.2.k.text: Link to data: binomial for defectives; Poisson for defects; normal, lognormal, and Weibull for continuous measures; t, F, and χ² are the sampling distributions behind the tests
3.1.2.k.title: Which distribution goes with which data

3.1.2.l.text: Weibull shape β: below 1 early failures, 1 random (exponential), above 1 wear-out. Hypergeometric applies when sampling without replacement from a small population (n about 5% of N or more).
3.1.2.l.title: Weibull shape and the hypergeometric

3.2.1.a.text: Inference: drawing conclusions about a population from a sample
3.2.1.a.title: What inference is

3.2.1.c.text: CI for a mean: x̄ ± t(α/2, n−1) × s/√n
3.2.1.c.title: Confidence interval for a mean

3.2.1.e.text: Interval width: shrinks with larger n, grows with higher confidence and higher variation
3.2.1.e.title: What makes the interval wider or narrower

3.2.1.f.text: A 95% CI means the method captures the true value in 95% of repeated samples. It is not "95% chance this interval contains it."
3.2.1.f.title: What "95% confidence" means

3.2.1.g.text: Use z when σ is known, t when σ is estimated
3.2.1.g.title: z or t?

3.2.1.i.text: Which change narrows the interval? Increase sample size.
3.2.1.i.title: Which change narrows the interval?

3.2.1.j.text: CI for a proportion: p̂ ± z × √(p̂(1 − p̂) / n)
3.2.1.j.title: Confidence interval for a proportion

3.2.1.k.text: t tables (reference document): Table 1 columns are cumulative probabilities 0.600 to 0.995 (headed "Alpha Risk" but equal to 1 − α). Table 2 columns are one-tail α (0.25 to 0.005) with more decimals. Rows are df = n − 1 for 1 to 30, then 40, 60, 120, ∞. Two-tailed α = 0.05 uses the 0.975 column (Table 1) or 0.025 (Table 2); one-tailed uses 0.950 or 0.05. For an unlisted df use the next lower listed df.
3.2.1.k.title: Reading the t table

3.2.2.a.text: Random, stratified, systematic, cluster, convenience, judgment
3.2.2.a.title: The methods

3.2.2.b.text: Stratified when the population has distinct subgroups; systematic = every kth unit
3.2.2.b.title: When to use which

3.2.2.c.text: Sample size for a mean: n = (Zα/2 · σ / E)²
3.2.2.c.title: Sample size for a mean

3.2.2.d.text: Sample size for a proportion: n = Z² p(1−p) / E²
3.2.2.d.title: Sample size for a proportion

3.2.2.e.text: Sample size depends on α, power, variation, and the smallest difference worth detecting
3.2.2.e.title: What drives sample size

3.2.2.g.text: Identify the sampling method from a description (every 10th unit = systematic).
3.2.2.g.title: Name the method from the description

3.2.2.h.text: Two kinds of sample size: precision for an estimate (formulas above) vs power for a hypothesis test (needs α, power, σ, and the smallest difference worth detecting)
3.2.2.h.title: Two kinds of sample size

3.2.2.i.text: 1-sample t: n ≈ (Zα/2 + Zβ)² σ² / δ². 2-sample t, equal n per group: n ≈ 2(Zα/2 + Zβ)² σ² / δ². n rises with σ and power, falls with δ and α.
3.2.2.i.title: Sample size for a hypothesis test

3.2.3.a.text: Sample means tend toward a normal distribution as n increases, regardless of the population shape
3.2.3.a.title: The statement

3.2.3.b.text: Mean of sample means = μ. Standard error = σ/√n.
3.2.3.b.title: Mean and standard error

3.2.3.c.text: n ≥ 30 is a classroom heuristic only; the n needed depends on skewness, tails, and outliers
3.2.3.c.title: How large is large enough?

3.2.3.d.text: Why Xbar charts and t-tests work reasonably with non-normal data
3.2.3.d.title: Why it matters

3.2.3.e.text: CLT does not make individual values normal
3.2.3.e.title: What it does not do

3.2.3.f.text: Compute the standard error and probabilities for a sample mean
3.2.3.f.title: Probabilities for a sample mean

3.2.3.g.text: σ = 10, n = 25 gives SE = 2. A common trap is using σ instead of SE for a mean.
3.2.3.g.title: σ versus standard error

3.3.1.a.text: H0: no difference, status quo, equality. Ha: the claim you are looking for evidence of (≠, <, >).
3.3.1.a.title: The hypotheses

3.3.1.b.text: Steps: practical problem, hypotheses, choose α, choose test, sample size, collect data, test statistic and p-value, decision, practical conclusion
3.3.1.b.title: The steps

3.3.1.c.text: p-value: probability of data this extreme if H0 were true. If p < α, reject H0.
3.3.1.c.title: The p-value

3.3.1.d.text: Never "accept H0." Say "fail to reject H0."
3.3.1.d.title: Wording the conclusion

3.3.1.e.text: One-tailed vs two-tailed; independent vs paired samples
3.3.1.e.title: One-tailed or two-tailed; independent or paired

3.3.1.f.text: CI and test agree: a CI that excludes the hypothesized value means reject H0
3.3.1.f.title: Confidence intervals and tests agree

3.3.1.g.text: p = 0.08 with α = 0.05: fail to reject. Watch the conclusion wording.
3.3.1.g.title: Careful with the wording

3.3.2.a.text: Huge samples can make trivial differences statistically significant
3.3.2.a.title: Huge samples find tiny differences

3.3.2.b.text: Small samples can miss large, real differences
3.3.2.b.title: Small samples miss big differences

3.3.2.d.text: Practical significance asks whether the difference matters to the business or the customer
3.3.2.d.title: Practical significance

3.3.2.e.text: p = 0.001, but the difference is 0.01 mm inside tolerance: statistically significant, not practically significant.
3.3.2.e.title: Significant but not important

3.3.2.f.text: p = 0.07 with low power and a large observed effect: 'insufficient evidence; check power and sample size,' not 'no difference'
3.3.2.f.title: Not significant, but not proven the same

3.3.3.a.text: Type I (α): reject a true H0; false alarm; producer's risk
3.3.3.a.title: Type I error (α)

3.3.3.b.text: Type II (β): fail to reject a false H0; missed detection; consumer's risk
3.3.3.b.title: Type II error (β)

3.3.3.c.text: Power = 1 − β. Typical α = 0.05, power = 0.80 to 0.90.
3.3.3.c.title: Power

3.3.3.f.title: Name the error

3.3.3.g.title: Producer's and consumer's risk

3.3.4.a.text: Selection depends on: data type, number of groups, normality, and the parameter (mean/median, variance, proportion)
3.3.4.a.title: What selection depends on

3.3.4.b.text: Normal, mean: 1-sample t (or Z), 2-sample t, paired t, one-way ANOVA
3.3.4.b.title: Normal data, means

3.3.4.c.text: Normal, variance: 1-sample variance (chi-square), 2 variances (F-test), several (Bartlett, Levene)
3.3.4.c.title: Normal data, variances

3.3.4.f.text: Parametric vs non-parametric. Non-parametric tests often have lower power when the parametric model holds. The BOK splits normal-data and non-normal-data testing, so the exam default is the normal vs non-normal fork; robustness nuances (large-n t-tests, shape assumptions) sit on top of it.

3.4.1.h.text: Reference-sheet versions: Welch df = (A + B)² / [A²/(n1 − 1) + B²/(n2 − 1)] with A = s1²/n1, B = s2²/n2; pooled s_p = √[((n1 − 1)s1² + (n2 − 1)s2²) / (n1 + n2 − 2)]; 2-sample Z when the σ's are known. The sheet's df subscripts are generic; pooled df = n1 + n2 − 2.

3.4.3.b.title: Why not several t-tests?

3.4.3.c.title: The ANOVA relationships

3.4.3.e.title: Assumptions

3.4.3.f.text: ANOVA says "at least one differs," not which. Use post-hoc (Tukey, Fisher, Dunnett) or interval plots.

3.4.3.g.title: What the topic includes

3.4.3.i.title: Bartlett versus Levene

3.4.3.j.text: A significant ANOVA means at least one mean differs. Do not name the largest sample mean the winner without post-hoc evidence. In Tukey/Fisher pairwise intervals, an interval containing 0 means no evidence of a difference.

3.4.3.k.text: Sample size and power for ANOVA: inputs are number of levels, the smallest difference between means worth detecting, σ, α, and power
3.4.3.k.title: Sample size and power for ANOVA

3.4.3.l.text: F tables (reference document): upper-tail critical values for α = 0.05, 0.01, and 0.10, each in two parts. Columns are numerator df (1 to 10, then 12, 15, 20, 24, 30, 40, 60, 120, ∞); rows are denominator df. The ANOVA F test is upper-tailed. For a two-sided variance test, put the larger variance in the numerator; the α = 0.05 table gives a two-sided test at α = 0.10, and there is no α = 0.025 table.
3.4.3.l.title: Reading the F table

3.4.3.m.text: ANOVA by hand (reference sheet): C = T²/N; SS_total = ΣX² − (ΣX)²/N (= ΣX² − C), or (N − 1)s²; SS_treatment = Σ(Tᵢ²/nᵢ) − C, or Σnᵢ·X̄ᵢ² − N·X̿², or for equal n n(k − 1)·s² of the group means; SS_error = SS_total − SS_treatment
3.4.3.m.title: ANOVA by hand with the reference-sheet formulas

5.2.10.g.text: Given a chart, identify the rule violated and decide the correct action (investigate vs leave alone).
5.2.10.g.title: Read the chart and choose the action

5.2.10.h.text: Anatomy: plotted statistic, center line, UCL/LCL at ±3σ of the plotted statistic, and zones A (2 to 3σ), B (1 to 2σ), C (center to 1σ) used by the sensitizing rules. σ of the data differs from σ of the statistic (σ/√n for subgroup means).
5.2.10.h.title: Anatomy of a control chart

5.2.10.i.text: Western Electric (8 in a row on one side) and Nelson/Minitab (9) are different rule systems, not contradictions. Use one set per question and do not mix them.
5.2.10.i.title: Two rule systems

5.2.10.j.text: Minitab applies only the beyond-limits test on time-weighted charts (EWMA, CuSum)
5.2.10.j.title: Time-weighted charts

5.2.10.k.text: Do not recompute limits because a point is out of control. Investigate the assignable cause; recompute only after a verified process change and a stable baseline.
5.2.10.k.title: Do not recompute limits just because a point is out

5.2.10.l.text: A point inside the 3σ limits can still violate a run or trend rule; 'all points within limits' does not prove control
5.2.10.l.title: Inside the limits is not the same as in control
